screens.title: Control Flow: Conditionals and Loops
screens.subtitle: Make decisions and repeat actions to create responsive gameplay

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how scripts decide what to do next and how to repeat tasks reliably. Control flow is the set of statements that let your code branch and loop: conditionals let you choose between paths, and loops let you repeat behavior. You will see practical patterns used in game scripts — checking player health, switching behavior by game state, spawning many objects, and safely using repeating loops without freezing the editor. The visual cards highlight three core topics you will master: conditional branching with if, else if, else and switch; repetition with for, while, do-while and foreach; and loop control using break and continue. Each concept includes a concrete Unity-oriented example so you can immediately try it in a scene: a health check that triggers game over, a switch on an enum to change difficulty, and a for loop to spawn coins. Keep an eye out for common mistakes: wrong ordering in if chains, off-by-one errors in for loops, and infinite while loops. By the end you will be ready to combine these tools to write adaptive gameplay logic that is clear, efficient, and safe.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Control flow turns static scripts into interactive game systems. Learning it helps you implement game rules, manage states, and spawn or iterate game objects safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement conditional logic and several looping constructs that are essential for Unity scripting. First, you will write clear if, else if and else blocks to respond to game state changes, such as player health thresholds. Second, you will use switch statements to select behavior when a variable has several fixed values, like an enum for game state or power-up type. Third, you will construct for, while, and do-while loops to repeat actions, knowing when each shape is appropriate. Finally, you will iterate collections safely with foreach and control loop execution with break and continue. Each objective includes a practical reason: conditional logic makes gameplay reactive, switch improves readability, loops let you spawn and update many objects, and loop controls help you skip or exit iterations cleanly. You will practice these skills by creating a GameLogicManager script that demonstrates health checks, difficulty-based spawning, countdowns, and safe iteration. These abilities let you implement adaptive and efficient gameplay systems.

screens.title: How you'll apply these skills
screens.subtitle: Concrete tasks and why they matter in a Unity project

narration.text: These objectives are not abstract. You will implement a GameLogicManager script that demonstrates each control flow construct in a playable scene. For conditionals, you will implement a health-status check that logs or triggers game over when health reaches a threshold. For switch statements, you will change game behavior based on a difficulty enum so the code reads clearly and is easy to extend. For loops, you will spawn multiple objects with a for loop and practice avoiding off-by-one errors. For iteration tasks, you will use foreach to greet or update an array of player names safely. You will also practice safe loop termination by using Time. deltaTime or counters, and use break and continue to alter loop progress when certain conditions are met. These tasks mirror common tasks in real projects: managing state, instantiating objects, and iterating collections. Completing them improves your ability to write predictable, maintainable gameplay code and to debug common mistakes efficiently.

screens.title: If, Else If, Else — ordered decision making
screens.subtitle: Use boolean checks to select a single actionable branch

narration.text: An if statement runs a block of code only when its boolean condition is true. When you need multiple exclusive branches, chain if, else if, and else. The chain is evaluated top to bottom. Once a condition is true, that branch runs and the rest are skipped. This ordering matters for ranges and thresholds. For example, when checking player health for messages, place the highest thresholds first. If you test a broader condition before a narrower one, the narrower case may never run. A practical health example is provided in the GameLogicManager: several else if checks map numeric ranges to messages from 'defeated' to 'full health'. A common mistake is incorrect logical operators or reversed order. Another error is duplicating overlapping ranges that create unreachable branches. Test by changing the value in the Inspector and watching the Console output. Also, think about performance: simple boolean checks are cheap, but complex logical expressions and heavy computations inside conditions should be avoided. As a takeaway, always structure your if chains from most specific to most general. Try a quick thought exercise: if you check whether score is at least 1000 before 100, what result do you expect for a score of 150? That ordering decision determines which message players see.

keyIdea.title: If-chain insight
keyIdea.text: Evaluate conditions from most specific to most general to avoid unreachable branches and surprising behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › If Chains
Definition
If / Else If / Else
Execute one branch based on the first true condition. Order affects which branch runs.
// Health status example if (playerCurrentHealth <= 0) { Debug.Log("Player is defeated! Game Over."); } else if (playerCurrentHealth <= 25) { Debug.Log("Player health is critical! Seek cover!"); } else if (playerCurrentHealth <= 75) { Debug.Log("Player health is stable. Keep fighting!"); } else { Debug.Log("Player is at full health. Ready for action!"); }
Key points
  • Chains run in order; the first true condition stops the chain.
  • Place narrow, high-priority checks before broader ranges.
  • Avoid overlapping ranges that make branches unreachable.
  • Keep heavy calculations out of condition checks for clarity and performance.
Key Takeaway

Order your conditions from most specific to most general. Test thresholds with example values to confirm behavior.

screens.title: switch vs. if-else chains
screens.subtitle: Choosing the clearer, more maintainable option for multiple fixed values

narration.text: When a single variable can take several distinct known values, a switch statement often reads better than a long chain of else ifs. A switch lists each case clearly and prevents deeply nested boolean logic. In Unity you often switch on enums like game state or difficulty. For example, switching on a Difficulty enum lets you set spawn counts or enemy behavior per level. Each case ends with a break to avoid running into the next case. A common misconception is that switch always performs faster; compilers may optimize switches, but readability and intent should guide your choice. Another pitfall is forgetting break in languages where fall-through is allowed; in C# leaving out break when a case has code will cause a compiler error unless the case body is empty. Use default to catch unexpected values. When you have ranges or complex boolean combinations, if-else is still appropriate because switch requires constant values per case. As a practical exercise, model different outcomes for Easy, Medium, Hard, and Extreme difficulty levels with a switch and verify the spawned count logic. Which construct you choose affects maintainability, so prefer switch for distinct fixed options and if-else for ranges or compound conditions.

keyIdea.title: When to switch
keyIdea.text: Use switch for many distinct constant cases. Use if-else for ranges or complex conditions.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Switch vs If
Switch example (enum)
public enum Difficulty { Easy, Medium, Hard, Extreme } switch (gameDifficulty) { case Difficulty.Easy: coinsToSpawn = 5; break; case Difficulty.Medium: coinsToSpawn = 10; break; case Difficulty.Hard: coinsToSpawn = 15; break; case Difficulty.Extreme: coinsToSpawn = 20; break; default: coinsToSpawn = 10; break; }
Each case maps a constant value to a behavior. Use default to handle unexpected values.
Comparison: when to choose
  • Switch: many fixed values, clearer case labels, easier to read and maintain.
  • If-Else: ranges, compound boolean logic, or checks involving comparisons.
  • Performance: readability is primary; compiler optimizations vary by language.
Pro Tip

Prefer switch for enums and discrete types. Reserve if-else for ranges and complex predicates.

screens.title: for loops and off-by-one errors
screens.subtitle: Repeat a known number of times with a reliable counter

narration.text: The for loop is ideal when you know how many iterations you need. It has an initialization, a condition, and an iterator. A typical pattern in Unity is spawning objects: initialize a counter at zero, loop while the counter is less than the desired count, and increment the counter each iteration. A frequent mistake is an off-by-one error. If you write the condition incorrectly, you may spawn one too many or one too few objects. For example, looping with i <= count when i starts at zero will run count plus one times. To test, spawn five objects and confirm their number in the Scene or Console. Another practical detail is index usage when accessing arrays: valid indices run from zero to length minus one. Using i < array. Length ensures safety. Keep the loop body focused and avoid heavy allocations there; instantiating many objects at once can be expensive, so consider pooling for performance. The provided SpawnEnemies example shows the classic pattern and a debug log per spawn to help you verify behavior. As a learner, practice changing initialization, condition, and iterator to see how each affects the iteration count and the resulting scene.

keyIdea.title: Loop pattern
keyIdea.text: Use for when iteration count is known. Check condition boundaries to avoid off-by-one mistakes and index errors.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › for Loop
Code walkthrough
void SpawnEnemies(int count) {
  for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) {
    Instantiate(enemyPrefab, spawnPoint.position + new Vector3(i * 2, 0, 0), Quaternion.identity);
    Debug.Log("Spawned enemy #" + (i + 1));
  }
}
Confirm that if count is 5, loop runs five times. Change < to <= to observe the off-by-one error.
Safety checklist
  • Start counters at zero when indexing arrays from zero.
  • Use < length to avoid index out of range errors.
  • Log iteration counts during testing to confirm behavior.
  • Consider pooling for many instantiations to avoid spikes.
Common mistake

Using i <= count when starting at zero will run one extra iteration. Check boundaries carefully.

screens.title: while loops and infinite loop risks
screens.subtitle: Repeat until a condition changes — but ensure it will change

narration.text: A while loop repeats its body as long as its condition remains true. It's useful when the number of iterations is unknown and depends on runtime state, like a countdown or waiting for a flag. A common Unity use is a countdown variable reduced by time. However, while loops carry the risk of becoming infinite if the condition never becomes false. An infinite loop can freeze the editor, so always include a guaranteed exit path. For example, decrementing a timer by time since the last frame inside Update or a coroutine is fine. But inside Start, running a while loop that waits for an event without yielding can block the main thread. A do-while assures one execution before a condition is checked, which is useful for prompts that must run once. When using while, prefer adding a safety counter or timeout and consider using coroutines for time-based repetition. The example in the chapter uses a countdown that logs remaining time and ensures that the timer decreases. As practice, convert a while countdown into a coroutine and note how yielding prevents freezing. Remember the core rule: if the condition depends on changing state, make sure that state is updated inside the loop or via an awaited event.

keyIdea.title: Safety first
keyIdea.text: Ensure loop conditions can change. Use timeouts, counters, or coroutines to avoid freezing the editor.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › while & do-while
while loop example
while (timer > 0) {
  Debug.Log("Time remaining: " + timer);
  timer -= Time.deltaTime;
  if (timer <= 0) { Debug.Log("Time's up!"); }
}
If timer is never reduced, the loop will never end. In Unity, avoid blocking the main thread with long while loops.
Do-while and safety checks
Do-while runs at least once. Use it when the loop body must execute before the condition is checked, but still include limits and guard conditions to prevent runaway execution.
Try this

Convert a countdown while loop into a coroutine that yields each frame. Observe that the editor remains responsive.

screens.title: foreach loops for collections
screens.subtitle: Iterate elements directly without index management

narration.text: The foreach loop provides a concise way to process every element in a collection such as an array or list. Instead of managing an index variable, foreach assigns each element to a loop variable in turn. This reduces off-by-one errors and improves readability when you only need elements, not their indices. For example, greeting players stored in an array becomes simple and expressive. However, remember that foreach typically does not let you modify the collection structure while iterating; adding or removing items from the collection inside a foreach can throw exceptions or cause undefined behavior. If you need indices or to remove items safely, prefer a for loop or collect removals in a separate list to process afterwards. Another practical point is performance: foreach over arrays is efficient, but over some collection types it may allocate an iterator object. In Unity, use foreach for clarity when you merely visit elements and use for when you need an index or will mutate the collection. The sample Greetings example uses a string array and logs each name, which you can test by changing the array in the Inspector and running the scene.

keyIdea.title: Foreach rule
keyIdea.text: Use foreach to read every element cleanly. Avoid modifying the collection inside the loop; collect changes and apply them afterward.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › foreach
Example: greet players
public string[] playerNames = { "Alice", "Bob", "Charlie" };
void GreetPlayers() {
  foreach (string name in playerNames) {
    Debug.Log("Hello, " + name + "!");
  }
}
Foreach visits each element. If you need to remove items during iteration, collect them and remove after the loop to avoid errors.
When to use

Reading or applying a function to each element where indices are not required.

When to avoid

Modifying the collection structure while iterating. Use a for loop instead for safe removals.

screens.title: break and continue inside loops
screens.subtitle: Fine-grain control: exit or skip iterations

narration.text: Break and continue are tools to alter a loop's normal sequence. Break immediately exits the innermost loop and transfers control to the statement after that loop. Continue skips the remainder of the current iteration and begins the next one. Use break when you have met a condition that makes further work unnecessary, like finding a target or reaching a limit. Use continue to ignore certain items but still process later ones, such as skipping null entries. A common pattern is scanning a list and breaking when the target is found, which saves time. Another pattern is skipping invalid inputs with continue. The chapter gives an example loop printing numbers where continue skips printing a specific index and break exits when another index is reached. When using these statements, be mindful of nested loops: a break affects only the innermost loop. Overuse of break or continue can harm readability; prefer clear loop conditions when possible. As a practical exercise, instrument a for loop with both statements, observe console output, and reason about which iterations run. Ending question: did break or continue make the code clearer in your test, or did they obscure the loop logic?

keyIdea.title: Control flow tools
keyIdea.text: Use break to exit early and continue to skip an iteration. Apply them sparingly to keep code readable.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › break & continue
Example: skipping and exiting
for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
  if (i == 3) { continue; }
  if (i == 7) { break; }
  Debug.Log("Loop iteration: " + i);
}
// Output: 0,1,2,4,5,6
Continue skipped printing at index three. Break stopped the loop when index seven was reached.
When to break
Stop searching once a target is found to save work.
When to continue
Skip invalid or irrelevant items but keep scanning the rest.

screens.title: Build GameLogicManager: combined example
screens.subtitle: A guided code walkthrough tying conditionals and loops together

narration.text: The GameLogicManager ties the chapter's elements into one practical script you can run in a scene. It exposes playerCurrentHealth, a Difficulty enum, a coin prefab and a spawn origin. When Start runs, it prints checks, evaluates health with an if-else chain, applies difficulty settings via a switch, and spawns coins with a for loop. There is also a short while countdown to demonstrate time-based repetition. This combination shows real usage: conditionals decide state-based messages, switch assigns numeric behavior per enum, and the for loop creates multiple scene objects. Important testing steps are included: set fields in the Inspector, press Play, and inspect the Console and Scene view. If the coin prefab or spawn origin is missing, the script logs an error — that error message is deliberate and helps you debug inspector setup. As you adapt the script, try changing health values, switching difficulty, and varying spawn counts to see how each part interacts. Pay attention to ordering and safety: the spawn loop uses i < coinsToSpawn, and the while countdown decrements so it terminates. After running this example, reflect on where you might replace Instantiate with pooling for better performance.

keyIdea.title: Integrated practice
keyIdea.text: Combining conditionals, switch, and loops in one manager demonstrates how these constructs collaborate to implement game rules and spawning behavior.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › GameLogicManager
Starter script (excerpt)
public int playerCurrentHealth = 70;
public enum Difficulty { Easy, Medium, Hard, Extreme }
public Difficulty gameDifficulty = Difficulty.Medium;
public GameObject coinPrefab;
public Transform spawnOrigin;

void Start() {
  Debug.Log("--- Game Logic Checks ---");
  CheckPlayerHealthStatus();
  ApplyDifficultySettings();
  if (coinPrefab != null && spawnOrigin != null) { SpawnCoinsBasedOnDifficulty(); }
  else { Debug.LogError("Assign Coin Prefab and Spawn Origin in the Inspector!"); }
}
What to test
  • Change playerCurrentHealth to verify each health message.
  • Swap gameDifficulty to see different spawn counts.
  • Remove the prefab to trigger the inspector error message and practice debugging.
Key Takeaway

Integrate checks and loops in a manager script. Test interactions via the Inspector and Console to confirm expected runtime behavior.

screens.title: Design patterns for control flow in gameplay
screens.subtitle: Keep logic modular, readable, and testable

narration.text: Control flow should support maintainable systems. Rather than scattering ifs across many scripts, group related decisions. For example, a GameLogicManager can centralize health checks, difficulty application, and spawning. Use methods with clear names for each responsibility: CheckPlayerHealthStatus, ApplyDifficultySettings, and SpawnCoinsBasedOnDifficulty. This modular approach improves testability and makes unit tests or manual checks easier. Favor early returns to reduce nesting: if a required component is missing, log and return before deeper logic runs. Also separate decision data from behavior; for example, use a data structure or scriptable object to hold difficulty parameters and feed them into the switch or spawning logic. That reduces long switch statements in code and makes balancing easier. Another pattern is to keep heavy or time-consuming repetition inside coroutines or background systems that can yield and avoid blocking the main thread. Finally, document assumptions such as index ranges and expected inspector assignments so teammates can quickly understand why a condition exists. As a reflection, review your scripts and consolidate repeated condition checks into shared utilities or manager methods to reduce duplication and errors. Design patterns for control flow in gameplay means group related conditional and loop logic into named methods and use data-driven parameters to improve readability and balance.. In practical terms, keep logic modular, readable, and testable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Modular flow
keyIdea.text: Group related conditional and loop logic into named methods and use data-driven parameters to improve readability and balance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Design Patterns
Organize control flow
Keep decision logic modular, data-driven, and safe to run in the editor.
Single responsibility
Each method should do one thing: check health, apply settings, or spawn objects.
Data separation
Store parameters in scriptable objects or data classes rather than hard-coding them in switches.
Non-blocking loops
Use coroutines for time-based repetition or when yielding prevents freezing the main thread.
Refactor duplicated condition checks into utilities. Use early returns to make code flatter and easier to read. These choices reduce bugs and make gameplay behavior predictable during testing.

narration.text: These are the essential concepts to remember. Control flow governs which statements execute and in what order. Conditional statements let you choose code paths based on boolean expressions; use if, else if, and else for ranges and compound checks. The switch statement selects a branch based on a single value and reads clearly for enums and discrete cases. Loops repeat actions: for is for known counts, while and do-while for condition-driven repetition, and foreach for visiting collection elements. Use break to exit loops early and continue to skip the rest of the current iteration. Watch out for infinite loops, off-by-one errors, and modifying a collection while iterating. Keep logic modular and testable by splitting responsibilities into well-named methods and use inspector-driven parameters to tune behavior during testing. These reminders will help you apply conditionals and loops safely as you build interactive gameplay features.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: Conditionals and loops make your game responsive and repeatable. Use them with attention to ordering and safety.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Key Concepts
Control Flow
The order in which statements execute. Branch and repeat to build interactivity.
Conditionals
if, else if, else and switch. Decide which code path runs based on values or conditions.
Loops
for, while, do-while, foreach. Repeat actions; choose the form that matches your needs.
Summary
Use clear ordering, prefer modular methods, test with inspector values, and guard loops to prevent freezes.

narration.text: Keep a compact reference in mind as you code. If executes when a boolean is true. Else if and else extend that pattern for multiple exclusive outcomes. Switch expresses selection over many constant values and improves readability when working with enums. For loops repeat a known number of times and require correct boundary checks to avoid off-by-one errors. While and do-while run until a condition changes, with do-while guaranteeing one execution. Foreach visits each element of a collection and avoids manual index handling. Break immediately exits a loop and continue skips to the next iteration. Finally, infinite loops arise when conditions cannot become false. These concise notes should guide debugging: check ordering for if chains, inspect boundaries for for loops, and verify state changes in while loops. What to Remember means short, precise reminders of each construct and the errors to watch for during implementation and testing.. In practical terms, short definitions for quick review. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compact review
keyIdea.text: Short, precise reminders of each construct and the errors to watch for during implementation and testing.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Quick Reference
If / Else
Ordered checks. First true branch runs and stops the chain.
Switch
Best for many discrete constant cases such as enums.
For / While / Do-While
Choose by whether count is known and whether you need at least one execution.
Final Tip

Always test control flow with representative values and check the Console output to verify expectations before iterating on complex logic.
